text: Welcome to Advanced Quantum Software Engineering. This course treats quantum programs as production code first, physics second. A circuit that runs in a notebook and looks right is not the same thing as software you can hand to a teammate, rerun six months later, or trust on real hardware.

Here's the shape of this lesson: why the notebook trap is so easy to fall into, the three failure modes that make quantum code genuinely different from typical classical code, how classical software engineering practices map onto a quantum codebase and where that mapping breaks, and what done actually means for a quantum function.

Quantum tutorials almost universally follow the same pattern: build a circuit, call dot run, print counts, done. That's fine for learning a gate. It's a bad habit for anything you intend to keep. A cell that printed a particular count split once, three weeks ago, proves nothing about whether the circuit is still correct after you refactored the oracle or upgraded a dependency. Treat a quantum function the way you'd treat a function calling a flaky third-party API: don't trust a single manual run, write tests that account for variability, and re-run them on every change.

Three properties of quantum programs mean you can't apply classical practices unmodified. First, measurement is inherently probabilistic — the same correct circuit gives different raw counts on different runs. Second, real hardware is noisy, and that noise profile drifts between calibration cycles. Third, the SDK ecosystem is unusually unstable — Qiskit's transition from the zero-point-x series to Qiskit one-point-oh removed and renamed core APIs, and other SDKs have had comparably disruptive transitions.

Classical practices still apply, they just need a quantum-specific adaptation. Unit tests with exact assertions still work for circuit construction, but measurement-outcome tests become statistical tests instead, which Chapter 2 builds in depth. Pinning dependency versions now means pinning the SDK version and recording the backend or simulator version together. And asking whether something fits in budget now means checking qubit count, circuit depth, and shot budget before you ever submit to hardware — Chapter 5's resource-estimation work.

By the end of this course, done for a quantum function means four concrete things are true: it has unit tests covering circuit construction that don't depend on measurement randomness at all; it has statistical tests covering measurement outcomes with an explicit, justified tolerance; its backend is injected rather than hardcoded, so the same logic runs in CI and in production; and its dependencies, random seed, and shot count are recorded alongside any result you report.

That's the bar this entire course is built around — not 'it printed a plausible histogram once,' but tested, documented, pinned, and reproducible. Next lesson, we start with the first piece: how to structure a real quantum software package, not a flat tutorial script.
